title.full: ASEAN Green Future Project Phase 2.1 & 2.2 Report, Decarbonisation Pathways for Singapore

publisher.full: Sustainable Development Solutions Network and ClimateWorks Centre

description: Singapore pathway to achieve near net-zero power sector emissions with a diversified power mix.
pathwayDescription:
The Highly Ambitious 2 Simulated (HA2S) scenario explores a pathway in which Singapore adopts a diversified mix of low carbon energy sources to achieve near net-zero in the power sector by 2050. This pathway is not a least cost optimization, but is built as a rules-based simulation consistent with achieving deep decarbonization by 2050 with a diversified mix of low carbon generation.

Rather than relying on a single dominant fuel or technology (as is more the case in the complementary Highly Ambitious 1 Simulated scenario from the same developers), HA2S develops a balanced portfolio that integrates multiple low-carbon energy sources. This includes large-scale imports of renewable electricity, the introduction of nuclear power for firm baseload generation, the deployment of advanced geothermal systems, and the gradual scale-up of low-carbon hydrogen and ammonia for dispatchable capacity. This diversified approach reduces dependence on any single fuel and improves system resilience, while still achieving near-zero emissions in the power sector by 2050.

The ASEAN Green Future regional research project is run by the United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network, Climateworks Centre, and local researchers from leading universities. The project develops national policy analysis and near-zero pathways that are meant to provide policy recommendations and support policy makers.

coreDrivers.policies: Fossil phase-out, high imports and solar deployment, nuclear and geothermal deployment, CCS, and road electrification drive HA2.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: There is no rigid emissions target, but the assumptions are designed to achieve near-zero emissions by 2050.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Common Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 2 (SSP2) macroeconomic and sector-growth assumptions expand demand and GDP.
coreDrivers.behavioralShifts: Smart-meter response and a modeled shift to fully electric road vehicles reduce end-use energy intensity.
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: Compared to the complementary HA1 pathway, HA2 uses a diversified generation mix with nuclear, geothermal, solar, and a larger share of inputs to decarbonize.

dependencies.dependency_description: Fossil fuels are phased-out by 2050. The retiring gas fleet is replaced by renewable capacity with policy-set start dates: 200 MW hydrogen and 60 MW ammonia from 2027, 330 MW solar from 2031, 338 MW imports from 2032, 300 MW SMR nuclear and 50 MW geothermal from 2040. The binding policy constraint is whether the enabling framework for imports, nuclear and geothermal exists by those dates.

HA2S’ economic exposure lies in the price and commercial durability of imported electricity. Imports supply around half of 2050 generation at purchase prices that, per the report’s own table, vary threefold across Malaysia, Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam and Indonesia. The report states that cross-border renewable trade, while attractive, carries risks from undersea cable engineering and high interconnection costs, citing the failed Sun Cable project as the worked example.

HA2S depends on scale up of SMR nuclear plants  and deep geothermal. SMRs and floating nuclear plants remain 'politically challenging to deploy in and around Singapore'. A 2012 pre-feasibility study states nuclear was not sufficiently risk-proof for a state of Singapore's size and density, and that deep geothermal requires invasive drilling. However, a mid-2021 survey reports about 60% of young Singaporeans support nuclear. Regional nuclear ambitions (ID, PH, VN) may normalise the technology.

Cars and taxis reach 50% hybrid and 50% fully electric by 2040 and then 100% fully electric by 2050; buses and freight trucks go from 70% electric in 2040 to 100% by 2050; LPG cookers and natural-gas water heaters are phased out after 2030 so that all cooking and water heating is electric by 2050, displacing the 62% of households assumed to use town gas; and domestic shipping ends at 25% each of fully electric, biodiesel, methanol and low-carbon ammonia.

Import capacity reaches 7.7 GW in 2050. The report is direct about the risk this carries: undersea cable engineering and high interconnection costs 'may be a setback, as seen in the failed Sun Cable project to import 1.75 GW from Australia'. No storage is modelled, which is notable because HA2 pairs a high import share with a mix whose domestic component is largely variable. The report performs no curtailment, flexibility or grid-integration analysis.

HA2S depends on technology readiness levels improving for hydrogen/ammonia supply, SMRs, EGS/AGS, and CCUS, all of which were either not commercially viable when the report was released, or technological and safety concerns were raised.

HA2S leans heavily on energy imports (49.9% of 2050 electricity), with resulting import capacity needs of 7.7 GW. EMA conditional approvals cover only 4.2 GW. 3.5 GW of the requirement currently unaccounted for. Biomass consumption (using imported wood pellets) rises more than threefold. Nuclear fuel is an import dependency and classifed as non-renewable. Domestic solar remains below maximum technical potential, domestic geothermal additions planned, but potential is unexplored.
